judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's numeric claims all hold. I recomputed both residuals (73 − (5·5+47) = 1 and 44 − (5·5+25) = −6), both residual ranges (Plot A: 1 − (−1) = 2; Plot E: 8 − (−7) = 15), and both means (273/8 = 34.125 with the outlier, 263/7 = 37.571… → 37.57 without, a shift of about 3.4). I also checked something the judge asserts but does not evidence — that the plot judgements rest on the same numbers the checks use. They do: worksheet.tex line 35 plots (1,52) and line 42 plots (8,88), which are exactly the values verify.json id 1 compares, and the Plot A residual list printed in problem 7 has 1 in the fifth position, matching problem 4(a)'s residual at x = 5. That consistency is hand-maintained, not generated: gate_log.txt records `render-figures SKIPPED(no figure problems)`, so these pgfplots coordinates are typed into the .tex and only spot-checked by the prose heuristic. Where I part company is the answer key. The delivered Quick Answers bank reads '1. —' and '2. —'. Those are VERIFIED compare relations (expected '<' and '>', both PASS), printing the same em dash that problem 10 — a genuine manual item — prints. That is the canonical quick-answer-bank-drops-relation-answers defect, confirmed here for a second task beyond curr-044, and it is exactly the situation where a grader cannot tell 'verified' from 'nobody checked this'. The judge scored answer_key_quality 4 without noting it. I also read the 'eight mostly sparse worksheet pages' remark against the build's own model: page_budget computes 216.0cm of content, an ideal of 10 pages and an accepted range of 7-12 (gate_log.txt line 96-98), so the delivered 8 pages is two pages UNDER what the system says this content deserves. I would not have taken the visual point off.

strengths_to_preserve: The sheet's organising rule — every problem asks for a number first and a description second, and the description has to cite the number — is enforced in the artifact, not just announced: problem 4 computes one residual on each of two plots before asking which point sits closer, and problem 7 supplies both full residual lists so 'strength' becomes the range 2 versus the range 15.

Plots A and E are built with the SAME trend slope of 5 and different residual spreads. That is the single most effective design decision on the sheet: it makes 'strength is not slope' a computation rather than an assertion, and problem 10 then asks the student to judge a 'strong link' claim using the ranges rather than the steepness.

Problem 5 is the case where the end-point method correctly reports nothing — Plot C's highest and lowest y sit next to each other in the middle (x = 6 and x = 5) — so the technique taught in problems 1 and 2 is shown failing to find a direction instead of being quietly dropped.

Problem 6 declares its misconception trap (reading the smallest x, value 1, instead of the x carrying the smallest y, 7) and the verifier proved it distinguishable, so the printed 'common wrong answers' line tells a grader which mistake produced a 1.

root_causes.description: render_quick_answers.py::_fmt sends every string expected through bare sympy.sympify. sympify('<') raises, the except branch returns '---', and '---' is also what render_entry returns for a manual-only id. Two different verification states — proved correct, and deliberately not machine-checkable — are printed with one glyph.
evidence: verify.json id 1: {"type": "compare", "values": ["52", "88"], "order": "relation", "expected": "<"}; id 2 is the same with '>'.
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers: '1. —', '2. —', beside '10. —', which is the genuine manual item.
scripts/render_quick_answers.py lines 57-61 and 74-76: the SympifyError fallback and the manual-only fallback return the same string.

root_causes.description: Nine of the ten problems print a lettered prose part that a human must read — and only problem 10 carries a manual entry. Because each of those problems also carries a numeric check, the id looks covered, and the sheet reports itself as 'thirteen checks cover problems 1 through 9' when in fact each of those nine also carries an ungraded written response.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 1(b) 'State the direction … and say how your comparison in (a) supports it'; 3(b) 'Describe in words what they do'; 4(c) 'Which of the two points sits closer … and how do you know'; 5(c) 'explain why Plot C has no association'; 6(b)-(c) 'describe the direction, form and strength of what is left' and 'Explain in one sentence'; 7(b) 'explain what the range … is actually measuring'; 8(b) 'Explain why the conclusion is still wrong, using the word form'; 9(c) 'Say what that shows'.
verify.json contains exactly one manual entry, on id 10.
answer_key.pdf carries per-problem 'Grading note:' lines for several of these, which is proof the author knew they need human reading.

improvements.title: Render verified comparison relations in the bank instead of the manual em dash
improvements.proposed_change: In render_quick_answers.py::_fmt, special-case relation strings before sympify: map '<', '>', '<=', '>=', '=', '!=' to their LaTeX glyphs and, when the entry is a `compare` with an `order`/`values` pair, print the full comparison ('$52 < 88$') so the row is readable on its own. Reserve '---' strictly for ids whose only entries are manual, and mark those rows explicitly (e.g. '— (manual)') so a grader can never confuse 'verified' with 'unchecked'.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture verify JSON with id 1 = compare/expected '<' (PASS) and id 2 = manual. Assert today's generator emits the same text for both rows (it does — curr-246's shipped bank shows '1. —' beside '10. —'); after the fix, row 1 must contain the '<' glyph and row 2 must be the manual marker, and the two must differ.
improvements.expected_impact: Every verified answer becomes visible in the grading strip; the em dash regains its single meaning. Affects every sheet using compare entries — the direction/inequality items across the statistics and number-sense bands.
improvements.risk: Low. The only care needed is column-width: 'compare' rows become longer, and column_count() picks 4/3/2 columns from the widest entry, so the fixture should assert the bank still lays out in at least two columns.

improvements.title: Declare the written half of every number-then-describe problem as manual
improvements.proposed_change: For a sheet built on 'compute first, describe second', each problem needs BOTH kinds of entry: the numeric check and a manual entry carrying the acceptance criteria the answer key already prints as its 'Grading note'. Add the gate described under the systemic key — scan each \problem body for an imperative prose ask and require a manual entry on that id — and have final_response.md's verification paragraph be generated from the JSON so it cannot claim nine problems are covered when nine written responses are not.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture worksheet whose problem 1 renders '(a) … leftmost … rightmost' answer slots plus '(b) State the direction … and say how your comparison supports it', with a verify.json id 1 holding only the compare entry. The gate must fail naming id 1's part (b); adding a manual entry must make it pass. Today the shape builds green.
improvements.expected_impact: The manual-review count a teacher reads becomes true. On this sheet it moves from 1 item to 10, which is the honest number for a set whose whole point is that the description is the answer.
improvements.risk: Ten manual entries on a ten-problem sheet could read as 'nothing was verified'. The fix must keep the numeric checks visible in the same row so the report distinguishes 'partly verified, prose read by hand' from 'not verified at all'.

improvements.title: Cover the two read-off values in problems 1 and 2, not only the relation between them
improvements.proposed_change: worksheet.tex renders three response slots in each of problems 1 and 2 — 'leftmost~\ansblank \quad \underline{\hspace{1.2cm}} \quad rightmost~\ansblank' (lines 136 and 149) — while the compare entry supplies one expected, the relation. The two y-values the student reads off the plot survive only as the entry's `values` INPUTS, so a student who misreads Plot A's leftmost point as 55 and still writes '<' is scored correct by everything the pipeline knows. Add read_data entries pinning the leftmost and rightmost y-values against the same data array that draws the plot, and have the coverage gate compare the count of \ansblank plus response-rule macros in a \problem body against the number of expecteds bound to that id.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture worksheet whose problem renders three response macros (two \ansblank plus one \underline rule) with a verify.json id supplying a single compare expected. tests/check_layout.py must exit non-zero naming the two uncovered slots; today the identical shape passes, as curr-246's green gate_log.txt shows. The sibling fixture adding two read_data entries must pass.
improvements.expected_impact: The values a student physically writes on the sheet are all checked, and the bank can print them in reading order rather than a single relation glyph.
improvements.risk: Counting response macros will need to ignore decorative rules in the header and the name/date line; \underline{\hspace{...}} is used for both, so the counter should look only inside \problem bodies.

case_summary: A rigorous concept-models sheet whose central design choice — two plots sharing a trend slope of 5 with residual ranges 2 and 15 — makes 'strength is not slope' something the student computes. All 14 checks recompute correctly, the pgfplots coordinates match the verify data point for point, and final_response.md names all three PDFs with their filenames. Two defects the verdict does not record: the Quick Answers bank prints '1. —' and '2. —' for two VERIFIED comparison relations, the same glyph as problem 10's genuine manual item; and nine of the ten problems require a written description that only a human can grade while only problem 10 is declared manual. The eight-page criticism runs against the build's own budget, which computes an ideal of ten pages for this content.
